newsitem.title: DENMARK: New Danish bonds seen squeezing six pct paper.
newsitem.headline: New Danish bonds seen squeezing six pct paper.

text.p: A flurry of short-maturity four percent bonds issued over the past week is likely to place some pressure on existing low-coupon paper in the next few months but analysts expect the overall impact to be limited.
The new bonds are a result of a recent lowering of the Copenhagen Stock Exchange bond rate floor, but the floor is seen rising again at the next scheduled evaluation, in December.
"Because of tax advantages with the low coupon these bonds primarily interest the private investor, so the amount that can be absorbed is limited," an analyst told Reuters on Tuesday.

"There is also a limited time before the next likely adjustment, but while the issuance window is open they are likely to syphon some funds from slightly more expensive paper," added the analyst, who asked not to be identified.

Unibank Senior Analyst Klaus Dalsgaard agreed that the potential volume was limited and he expected the floor to rise in December but said that four percent bonds would still trickle down through banks to private buyers after issuance ends.
"The next (adjustment) is very likely to be five percent. Five percent is great but four percent is better, so everybody is trying to issue as much as possible," he said.

"I would think it would take some time before all these new four percent bonds are placed with private individuals so I think we will see continued interest in, for example, selling the six percent 2002 and buying a new four percent bond in the coming months, so I think (six percent paper) will be a little bit under pressure for quite some time," Dalsgaard added.
The floor rate is normally fixed twice-yearly, in June and December, according to an average of yields on specified fixed-interest, government and mortgage-backed bonds over a fixed 20-day period.

It was left unchanged at six percent last June but reduced to four percent in an unscheduled adjustment on October 22, after several expiring mortgage-backed bonds were replaced by smaller series, reducing the average.

Borrowers, most of them foreign, quickly offered some five billion crowns worth of new four percent paper knowing that it was eagerly awaited by Danish private investors for whom the low coupon provides tax advantages.

"In general, these bonds give investors a return after tax that is one percentage point higher than is the case with government bonds," BG Bank department chief Joergen Blaunfeldt told the daily Berlingske Tidende on Tuesday.
"For Danish businesses they are, as a rule, not nearly so attractive because any market loss is not deductible as an operating expense," he added.
"If you take the Danish yield curve you'll see that traditionally foreigners would own perhaps 60 percent of some of the long-dated bonds," Dalsgaard said.

"But if you take a bond like the six percent 2002 or the six percent 1999 -- traditional 'tax bonds'-- they will primarily be owned by domestic investors and definitely we are going to see over the near future that they are going to switch to these new bonds, I'm sure about that," he added.
